extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in religion, deism, and critiques of the Bible/Christian theology
extracted.subtask_description: A critical evaluation of the Bible and Christian theology focused on authorship, genre, internal evidence, the nature of revelation, and what constitutes true theology or divine communication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prophesying as poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: The original meaning of 'prophesy' was the making or performance of poetry and music; the books called the Prophets are composed in poetical numbers rather than prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains two components of poetry—imagery and composition (meter). Argues that prophetic books show poetic imagery and metrical composition (mixing long and short syllables); gives examples (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and demonstrates by matching syllable counts and rhyme. Use meter and imagery to judge these writings as poetry rather than revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human language cannot be the vehicle of the Word of God
rubrics_metrics.description: Human language is local and changeable and therefore incapable of conveying an unchangeable, universal Word of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lists reasons: continual semantic change, lack of a universal language, translation losses and mistakes, copyist and printer errors, and the possibility of wilful alteration. Concludes that any purported written scripture cannot be the unalterable Word of God for these reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: The true Word of God is the Creation
rubrics_metrics.description: The only true, universal revelation (the Word of God) is the Creation itself, not any human-authored book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues the Creation is an ever-existing, universal 'scripture' that cannot be forged, altered, suppressed, or lost; it 'publishes itself' everywhere and reveals God's power, wisdom, munificence, and mercy. Recommends reading the works of creation to learn about God rather than human scriptures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be equal to the end — universal revelation requires adequate means
rubrics_metrics.description: To accomplish universal revelation to all nations, the means employed must be adequate; spoken Hebrew in the time of Jesus (and absence of printing) could not have communicated a universal, unchangeable revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the practical argument that Jesus spoke one language and printing was unknown, with hundreds of languages in the world, and translations inevitably lose or distort sense. Therefore a claimed universal written revelation from such means is implausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use internal evidence to assess authenticity when external evidence is lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: When external proof (contemporary authenticated texts) is unavailable due to distance in time, the credibility of doctrines or scriptures must be judged by their internal evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to the New Testament and doctrines like redemption: points to internal inconsistencies, stylistic signs, and conceptual bases (e.g., doctrinal ideas that align with pecuniary motives) as strong presumptions of fabrication. Notes church's proven capacity to fabricate or alter writings and that internal analysis (consistency, moral logic, correspondence to motives) is the available test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and moral character are criteria for divine authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: If large portions of a book contain obscene stories, cruelty, vindictiveness, or material that brutalizes mankind, this is strong evidence against its being the Word of God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author treats prevalence of immoral or brutal accounts in parts of the Bible as weighty negative evidence; recommends assessing the moral tenor of a text as part of judging its claim to divine origin.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess authenticity by authorship, dating, and provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims of revelation require scrutiny of who wrote the books and when; absence of writings authenticated by the purported author (e.g., Jesus) and books written after the subject's death undermine claims of direct revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes that the four Gospels are anecdotal, written after Jesus's death, and that authorship/original language are uncertain; uses such provenance factors to question revelatory claims and authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: True theology is the study of God's works (natural philosophy), not human opinions
rubrics_metrics.description: Theology properly consists of studying the works of creation (natural philosophy/science), from which knowledge of God and scientific principles is derived, rather than studying human writings and opinions about God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that contemplation of creation led to discoveries underlying sciences (trigonometry, astronomy, geometry, mechanics) and that calling sciences 'human inventions' is fraudulent. Cites Job and Psalm 19 as examples of deistical/theological writings that take the Creation as the word of God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrines must be morally coherent — critique of redemption as pecuniary idea
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid religious doctrine must be coherent with moral justice; a theory (such as redemption by one person suffering for another) that rests on a pecuniary/debt metaphor is morally incoherent for criminal justice and signals fabrication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the distinction between paying a debt (pecuniary) and suffering for a crime (moral justice) to argue that substitutionary redemption is conceptually flawed. Treats the pecuniary conception of sin/redemption as evidence the doctrine was fabricated to support financial mechanisms (indulgences, pardons) in the church.
